differences.title: 1. ORIGIN & COMPATIBILITY
differences.leftDesc: Valkey is a community-driven continuation of Redis’ codebase, emphasizing governance and compatibility. It targets a largely Redis-compatible command and protocol surface, but forks can diverge in edge behaviors over time.
differences.rightDesc: Redis is the original upstream project with a long-lived release cadence and mature operational tooling. Command semantics and module ecosystems tend to be tightly coupled to Redis’ own compatibility guarantees and versioning policy.

differences.title: 2. REPLICATION MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Both systems use primary-to-replica propagation for high throughput, typically async replication with PSYNC-style synchronization and incremental replication after full resync. Failover behavior depends on configuration and orchestration layer.
differences.rightDesc: Redis replication is well-understood: primaries stream replication commands to replicas, with full sync via RDB transfer when needed. Incremental updates rely on backlog windows and replica offsets for efficient catch-up.

differences.title: 3. PERSISTENCE & DURABILITY
differences.leftDesc: Valkey supports Redis-like persistence patterns: periodic snapshots (RDB) and append-only logs (AOF). Under the hood, it must coordinate background saves, fsync policies, and rewrite mechanics to balance latency and recovery time.
differences.rightDesc: Redis persistence is heavily battle-tested across RDB snapshots and AOF with configurable fsync frequency and log rewrite. The server’s background fork/write behavior is designed to minimize pause time while preserving recovery guarantees.

differences.title: 4. CLUSTERING & SHARDING
differences.leftDesc: Valkey cluster mode shards keys across nodes using a hash slot model and routing tables maintained via cluster messages. Resharding, node joins, and migrations require consistent slot ownership and transient forwarding behavior.
differences.rightDesc: Redis Cluster also uses hash slots for deterministic key placement, with node discovery via cluster gossip/meet protocols. Slot migrations involve coordinated handoffs and client redirection semantics to keep routing correct during movement.

differences.title: 5. MEMORY MANAGEMENT
differences.leftDesc: Both rely on efficient in-process allocation strategies for hot key/value workloads, using Jemalloc-style allocators in common builds. Eviction policies and object layout directly influence fragmentation, tail latency, and GC-like memory reclamation costs.
differences.rightDesc: Redis’ memory subsystem is tuned for predictable performance: object encoding choices (e.g., compact lists/sets) reduce footprint, while allocator and eviction strategies affect fragmentation. Under pressure, eviction and lazy freeing determine latency spikes.

differences.title: 6. LATENCY PATHS & COMMAND HOT LOOPS
differences.leftDesc: Valkey’s core request processing is a single-threaded command execution loop with multiplexed I/O, so throughput comes from minimizing per-command overhead, efficient parsing, and avoiding blocking calls. CPU hot paths are critical for tail latency.
differences.rightDesc: Redis uses a similar architecture: a single-threaded main loop executes commands deterministically, while I/O is handled via an event-driven model. Optimizations like fast object encoding and streamlined reply generation keep micro-latency low.

differences.title: 7. ECOSYSTEM & MODULE COMPAT
differences.leftDesc: Valkey’s module API compatibility aims to mirror Redis, enabling many existing modules to compile and run with fewer changes. Differences can surface in internal symbols, replication hooks, and persistence integration points.
differences.rightDesc: Redis has a large, mature module ecosystem (e.g., search, time series, and custom data structures). Modules often rely on Redis internals and specific build flags, so upgrading Redis can require coordinated module compatibility testing.
